scenes.narration: On August eleventh, twenty twenty, Citibank meant to pay about seven point eight million dollars of interest on behalf of the cosmetics company Revlon. Instead, it sent almost nine hundred million dollars of its own money. A federal judge later called it one of the biggest blunders in banking history. And then he ruled that much of the money did not have to come back.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Why was Citibank paying Revlon's bills at all?

In twenty sixteen, Revlon borrowed one point eight billion dollars through a syndicated loan. That means the money did not come from one bank, but from dozens of lenders, mostly investment funds. Someone has to sit in the middle, collect Revlon's payments and pass them on to every lender. That job is called the administrative agent. And Revlon's agent was Citibank.

Let me draw the plumbing. Here is Revlon. Here is Citibank, the agent. And here are the lenders. When an interest payment is due, Revlon sends the money to Citibank, and Citibank splits it and sends each lender its share. The agent does not lend. It only moves the money. But that means the agent's computers are connected to the bank's own vault. If the agent sends too much, the extra comes out of Citibank's own pocket.

scenes.narration: By twenty twenty, Revlon was in deep trouble. In May, it raised more than eight hundred million dollars in new financing, partly by moving assets that had protected the old loan into a new deal. Many lenders were furious. On the market, the old loan was trading for less than thirty cents on the dollar. In other words, investors doubted they would ever be paid back in full.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: Then, late on a Tuesday in August, Citibank paid them back in full. By accident.

keyframes.label: Then Citibank paid them back in full

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: How do you send nine hundred million dollars by mistake?

The task looked simple. As part of a deal with some of its lenders, Revlon had agreed to pay interest to all of its old lenders early. Citibank's payment software, called Flexcube, had an awkward quirk. The easiest way to send only the interest was to enter the transaction as if Revlon were paying off the entire loan, and then redirect the principal into an internal account, called a wash account, so that the money never left the bank.

keyframes.cue: as if Revlon were paying off
keyframes.label: items[2].at.cue

scenes.narration: According to the court, Citibank's own manual said that to keep the principal inside, three fields on the screen all had to be set to the wash account. They were called front, fund, and principal. The employee who built the payment, part of a team in India working for Citibank through the outsourcing firm Wipro, ticked only one. Principal.

keyframes.cue: part of a team in India
keyframes.label: items[3].at.cue

scenes.narration: Citibank had a safety rule for this, called six eyes. Three people must review a payment before it goes out. The second person checked it and approved. The third, a senior manager in the United States, replied, looks good, please proceed, principal is going to wash. All three believed the screen meant something it did not.

There was even a final warning. A box popped up saying the funds would be sent out of the bank, and asking, do you want to continue. But it did not say how much. And since the interest really was supposed to leave the bank, the warning looked normal. The approver clicked yes. And Citibank's money went out, matching, to the penny, everything Revlon owed on the loan.

Even the evidence went unread. That evening, as part of the routine, the employee who built the payment sent his manager the paperwork, including screenshots from the system. Under amount paid, they showed about seven point eight million dollars in interest, and eight hundred and ninety-four million dollars in principal. He did not see anything wrong, because he believed the system was showing the principal as paid into the bank's own internal account.

scenes.narration: Nobody noticed that evening. The next morning, somebody did.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Can you just ask for it back?

Around nine the next morning, a team manager checking the previous day's accounts found a discrepancy that should not have been there. In a chat message, one employee wrote, bad news, the wires look like they went out the door. By the afternoon, Citibank was sending notices to every lender, saying the money had been sent in error, and asking for it back.

Many lenders sent it back. About about three hundred and eighty-five million dollars came home. But ten investment firms, managing funds that had received more than five hundred million dollars, refused. One of them replied that it was not at all clear that the funds were paid in error.

Inside the funds, the reactions were telling. Some sent the money straight back. Others told their banks to wait. One firm said it was working with its lawyers to get approval to return the funds, but asked its trustee to hold off until it heard back. The longer they held on, the more it looked like a decision, not a delay.

keyframes.cue: Others told their banks to wait
keyframes.label: items[1].at.cue

scenes.narration: Why would they keep it? Look at it from their side. They held a loan the market valued at under a third of its face value. Suddenly, they had received every cent, in cash. And they were already in a fight with Revlon. The very next day, a group of lenders sued Revlon and Citibank over the May deal. To them, this money was not a gift. It was what they were owed.

scenes.narration: If someone pays you by mistake, do you have to give it back?

Usually, yes. Under New York law, a payment made by mistake generally has to be returned. But there is an old exception, called discharge for value. If you are owed money, and someone pays you that exact amount, and you had no reason to suspect a mistake, you can keep it. As New York's highest court once put it, you should be able to treat the payment as final.

If the answer to all three is yes, the arrow leads to keeping it. If any answer is no, the arrow leads back to the sender. The whole case came down to that third box.

scenes.narration: After a trial in December, Judge Jesse Furman ruled in February twenty twenty-one. The lenders, he found, could reasonably have believed the payment was deliberate. The amounts matched to the penny, and Revlon was backed by the billionaire Ronald Perelman, whose company owned about eighty-five percent of it. His conclusion was blunt. Citibank is not entitled to its money back. The lenders could keep about about five hundred and four million dollars.

For Citibank, it was an embarrassment on top of a bigger problem. The blunder raised questions about its controls, and, as the trade publication Banking Dive noted, it may have contributed to the four hundred million dollars fine that its regulator had imposed on the bank in October. Citibank said it would appeal.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: The appeal took another year and a half.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Should the lenders have known?

On September eighth, twenty twenty-two, the federal appeals court in New York reversed the ruling. First, the loan was not due until twenty twenty-three. So the lenders were not owed that money yet, and the old exception did not protect them.

Second, the court listed red flags that should have made any careful investor pick up the phone. Revlon had not sent the notice required for paying early. A struggling company was supposedly repaying everything three years ahead of time. It could have bought the same debt on the market for under thirty cents on the dollar. And days earlier, it had launched a deal designed to stop the loan from coming due early.

keyframes.cue: Revlon had not sent the notice
keyframes.label: items[0].at.cue

scenes.narration: The money had to go back. By then, the industry had already moved. Many loan contracts now include clauses saying that a payment made in error must be returned. And Revlon itself, the company at the center of it all, later filed for bankruptcy protection.

scenes.narration: So what does this story say about the money system? That the biggest transfers in the world still pass through a few people looking at a screen. Six eyes are only safe if each pair is really looking, not trusting the other two. A warning that does not show the amount is not much of a warning. And when money arrives that seems too good to be true, the law may one day ask a simple question. Why didn't you call?
